title: The Poisson Process
short: For random arrivals at rate λ, the count in a window of length t is Poisson with mean λt, and the gaps between arrivals are exponential with mean 1/λ.
trouble: Students give the count in time t the mean λ instead of λt, or give the gaps the mean λ instead of 1/λ.

blocks.html: The Poisson distribution counts random events in a window; the exponential distribution measures the wait between them. They are two views of the same model, the Poisson process: arrivals scattered in time at a steady rate, with no memory.

In a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$: the number of arrivals in any window of length $t$ is Poisson with mean $\lambda t$; counts in non-overlapping windows are independent; and the gaps between arrivals are independent exponential times with mean $\frac{1}{\lambda}$. The $k$th arrival comes after an expected $\frac{k}{\lambda}$.

Start the clock at any moment. The first arrival comes after time $t$ exactly when the window $[0, t]$ holds no arrivals, so $$P(\text{first wait} > t) = P(N(t) = 0) = e^{-\lambda t}:$$ the wait is exponential with rate $\lambda$. Because separate windows are independent, the same argument restarts after every arrival, so every gap is exponential and the gaps are independent. The time to the $k$th arrival is the sum of $k$ gaps, with mean $\frac{k}{\lambda}$ by linearity.

blocks.name: prob-poisson
blocks.cap: Arrivals at rate 2 per unit of time. The gaps between them form a histogram that follows the exponential density with mean one half.

blocks.title: Counts in a window
blocks.q: Customers arrive as a Poisson process at 6 per hour. Find the probability of exactly 2 arrivals in 20 minutes.
steps: 20 minutes is $\frac{1}{3}$ hour, so the mean count is $\lambda t = 6 \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 2$.

blocks.title: Waiting
blocks.q: With the same process, find the probability that nobody arrives in the next 15 minutes, and the expected wait for the 3rd customer.
steps: Each gap has mean $\frac{1}{6}$ hour = 10 minutes, so the 3rd arrival is expected after 30 minutes.

blocks.title: Given the total
blocks.q: Exactly 4 customers arrived during one hour. Find the probability that exactly 1 of them came in the first 15 minutes.
steps: Given the total, the 4 arrival times behave like 4 independent uniform points in the hour.
Each lands in the first quarter-hour with probability $\frac{1}{4}$, so the count there is binomial.

blocks.html: Giving the count in a window of length $t$ the mean $\lambda$ instead of $\lambda t$, or giving the gaps the mean $\lambda$ instead of $\frac{1}{\lambda}$. Check: a higher rate means more arrivals and shorter gaps, so the count's mean grows with $\lambda$ and the gap's mean shrinks.
